newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's PRI to select new string-pulling leader.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's PRI to select new string-pulling leader.

text.p: Mexico's long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) will chose an insider as its new leader this weekend in a bid to drag the party out of crisis after the resignation of Santiago Onate Labourde.

PRI officials said on Saturday that Humberto Roque Villanueva, a close ally of President Ernesto Zedillo, would register as the sole candidate to take over the presidency of the party that has governed the country for 67 years.

The PRI's national executive committee was expected to ratify Roque's candidacy when it meets on Sunday, paving the way for a new leadership thrust before crucial mid-term elections next year, they added.
Onate, who had led the PRI for 16 months, stepped down on Friday. In his letter of resignation, he said the time had come for a renewed leadership.

Interior Minister Emilio Chuayffet Chemor said the switch in leadership was aimed at redirecting the PRI prior to next summer's elections, where the challenge for the party is to hang on to its congressional majority.
"The PRI has to change even the way it walks," newspapers reported Chuayffet as saying.
Roque, the powerful 53-year-old PRI leader of the lower house of Congress, is known for his negotiating prowess, even with opposition congressmen.

Roque was heavily criticised recently for an uncouth gesture when he failed to control his delight after he won a tense vote to increase taxes. PRI congressmen had threatened to oppose the bill, but Roque dissauded them from toppling the presidential initiative.

In a television interview, Roque said recent desertions and state election setbacks had little impact on the party. "Changes in voting opinions and changes of opinion of party members must not shock us. What are important are strong convictions and the fundamental commitment to serve the public," Roque said.
His academic background is in economics, making him more akin to President Ernesto Zedillo's technocrat-filled Cabinet than Onate, who was much more a traditional career politician.

Roque cemented his friendship with Zedillo when the two worked closely together in the administration of ex-president Carlos Salinas. Roque was chairman of Congress's Planning and Budget Committee when Zedillo was deputy minister of that branch of the Finance Ministry.
Opposition parties decried the leadership change, saying it was window dressing covering up the PRI's internal crisis.

"They (the PRI members) want to put fresh paint on a building that is falling down, but they have to realise they cannot continue monopolising power," said Armando Quintero, a leader of the leftist Democratic Revolution Party.
Onate, a former labour minister, had come under fire recently because the PRI had suffered humiliating defeats in state elections in November and embarassing defections from the party.
